A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DiSRouter and retain matching core formulations, methods and experiments. The text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison despite reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original routing experiments, self-awareness evaluations, model-pool reduction tests and timing measurements in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds latency measurements, intrinsic self-awareness evaluations, heterogeneous-model routing and summarization experiments.

M1.justification: The original cascade and binary-task training pipeline remain. However, Appendix A.11.1 adds a substantive adaptation for continuous-quality tasks: SFT rejection thresholds become model-specific score percentiles, and RL uses continuous answer scores and percentile-based rejection rewards.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original ten datasets and adds harder mathematical reasoning evaluations on MATH-500, AIME 2024/2025, AMC 23, JEEBench, OlympiadBench and OlympicArena. It also adds summarization training and evaluation on SAMSum and XSum, extending coverage beyond the original verifiable question-answering tasks.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained experiments is unchanged, including RouteLLM, FrugalGPT, AutoMix, FORC and GraphRouter where applicable. Added routing studies reuse existing methods or subsets of them. Newly discussed methods such as AgentNet are not evaluated as additional baselines.

E3.justification: V2 adds GPT and heterogeneous-model configurations, a 100-query latency comparison, and BERTScore-based summarization evaluation with 12,000 training samples. Section 4.3 changes the reported rejected-query procedure from original-model answers to prefix-forced aligned-model answers. Appendix A.8 replaces the relative newly-solved-query metric description with ΔPass@10; identical plotted values do not establish that either retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses examine cumulative average and worst-case routing overhead, whether native rejection behavior suffices without alignment, and whether self-awareness and scenario adaptability transfer across model families and summarization tasks. These add substantial diagnostics beyond v1's retained modularity, difficulty-discrimination and training-capability analyses.

E5.justification: Figure 9 newly reports a 95% confidence band, Pearson correlation and a significance result for answer rate versus performance: r = 0.97 and p = 9.66e-05. Routing utility tables still lack repeated-run uncertainty reporting. The ten-response capability evaluation was already present in v1.

E6.justification: The original benchmark scores are retained, but substantial new results appear. Table 18 reports GPT-system utilities of 0.76 in-domain and 0.41 out-of-domain; Table 20 reports heterogeneous-system utilities of 0.71, 0.54 and 0.38 across the three scenarios. Additional results cover latency, native self-awareness and summarization. These are new evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: Appendix A.11 adds a continuous scoring definition, a percentile-based decision threshold in Equation 11 and its corresponding reward definition in Equation 12. The original routing formalization and reward-threshold derivation remain unchanged; the addition does not introduce a new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same scientific claims about distributed self-routing, independent self-awareness training, modularity and utility advantages. The added evaluations broaden supporting evidence without redefining these core statements.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations and applicability conditions: tested Qwen models require improved self-awareness, whereas sufficiently self-aware GPT models can route without alignment. It also discusses latency tradeoffs against predictive and cascading routers, and qualifies summarization applicability through metric saturation and dependence on a reliable quality signal.

D1.justification: V2 adds sequential timing details, GPT cost configurations, summarization's DeBERTa-based BERTScore setup and sample counts, and an intrinsic-rejection prompt. Existing training and baseline implementation recipes remain. The new prompt leaves its five example shots unspecified, and no new code or data release is documented.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds discussion of capability profiling, decoupled regression, early-abstention cascades and AgentNet's decentralized routing. References also expand for the new datasets, models and evaluation tools. These are focused extensions that retain the central positioning around intrinsic assessment versus external routers.

P1.justification: V2 adds an appendix contents page, reorganizes supplementary sections as A.1–A.12 and moves existing prompts/templates to the end. Selected method, generalization and related-work passages are rewritten; affiliations, publication headers and acknowledgments change. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the visual evidence with overhead, GPT, heterogeneous-model and summarization tables, plus Figures 9–12 containing correlation and self-awareness diagnostics. Table 6 gains a 14B column, Figure 8 receives revised metric labeling, and existing figures and appendix tables are relocated or renumbered.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for generality and practical efficiency. V1's routing evaluations used a homogeneous Qwen pool and its overhead argument relied on individual rejection times; v2 adds heterogeneous and GPT routing, summarization diagnostics, and cumulative/comparative latency measurements. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including the unreconciled Figure 8 metric change and Figure 10's AIME2025 exception to the claim of consistently higher answered-query accuracy.
